query:
Context: Our lab performs standards-based quantitative SEM-EDS (k-ratio protocol, NIST DTSA-II) at E0 = 5 keV on a Thermo Fisher Apreo FE-SEM with an EDAX Octane Plus SDD (takeoff angle 35 degrees). One standard is an UNCOATED bulk single-crystal MgO wafer (10 x 10 x 0.5 mm, epi-polished, mounted on a grounded aluminum stub, silver/carbon paint border planned at the edges). Our carbon evaporation coater is unavailable for two months. Scope: SEM / EPMA / electron-irradiation physics of BULK insulators and thin insulating films only; exclude TEM entirely.

Questions:

(1) DEPTH OF ELECTRON PENETRATION AND TRAPPED CHARGE IN CHARGING INSULATORS. What does the peer-reviewed literature say about how deep primary-beam electrons penetrate and where the injected charge actually comes to rest in an electron-irradiated bulk insulator? Cover: (a) the initial implantation depth versus beam energy (electron range scaling); (b) the depth DISTRIBUTION of trapped charge - the dynamic double layer picture (thin positive surface layer from secondary-electron escape over a deeper negative space-charge layer near the end of range), e.g. Melchinger & Hofmann 1995 J. Appl. Phys. 78:6224 'Dynamic double layer model'; Cazaux's analyses of internal fields and charge distributions (e.g. J. Appl. Phys. 59:1418, 1986); self-consistent charge-transport simulations such as the flight-drift model (Touzin, Goeuriot, Guerret-Piecourt, Juve, Treheux, Fitting, J. Appl. Phys. 99:114110, 2006) and Fitting's related work; (c) the SELF-REGULATION of landing energy: as negative surface potential builds, the landing energy falls toward the second total-yield crossover E2 so the penetration depth shrinks toward the range at E2 - published statements and measurements of this steady state; (d) experimental methods that measured trapped-charge depth or surface potential (electron-mirror method, Kelvin probe, x-ray/spectral methods, Duane-Hunt endpoint shifts) with quantitative example numbers.

(2) GROUNDING FROM BELOW: CONDUCTIVE LAYER UNDER A THIN INSULATOR INSTEAD OF A TOP COAT. Is there published work on analyzing or imaging uncoated insulators by placing the conductor UNDERNEATH - i.e., thin insulating films or sections on grounded conductive substrates charging far less than bulk insulators? Cover the physics quantitatively: capacitive scaling of surface potential with dielectric thickness over a ground plane (V proportional to thickness for a given trapped areal charge); electron-beam-induced (radiation-induced) conductivity within the irradiated volume allowing deposited charge to leak to a substrate that lies within or near the interaction volume; the condition that the beam range reach or approach the conductive layer; evidence from electron-beam lithography (insulating resist films ~0.1-1 um on grounded silicon wafers) and from SEM/EPMA practice (e.g., thermal SiO2 films on Si imaged/analyzed uncoated; thin sections on conductive substrates). Also: any work on deliberately BURIED conductive layers (implanted or deposited interlayers) for charge mitigation in SEM samples, and the known failure modes (fluorescence of the buried layer by X-rays generated above it; changed backscattering when the substrate is inside the interaction volume; thin-film versus bulk matrix-correction differences).

(3) MgO SPECIFICALLY AT LOW BEAM ENERGY. MgO has one of the highest secondary-electron yields of any material (used for exactly that property in plasma display panels). What are the measured secondary-electron yield curves (delta_max, E_max) and total-yield crossover energies E1 and E2 for MgO (single crystal, thin film, and degraded/contaminated surfaces), e.g. Whetten & Laponsky's classic measurements and later compilations (Joy's database of electron-solid interactions; Cazaux's reviews)? At E0 = 5 keV, does bulk single-crystal MgO sit ABOVE unity total yield (net positive, self-limiting few-volt positive charging - benign for EDS) or below it (negative charging by kilovolts)? How strongly do surface contamination, hydroxylation, and electron-beam conditioning shift delta and E2 for MgO? Any direct measurements of MgO surface potential or charging behavior under keV electron beams (including in SEM), and any published SEM-EDS or EPMA analyses of uncoated MgO?

(4) THE DUANE-HUNT ENDPOINT AS A CHARGING GAUGE. Published validation of using the bremsstrahlung continuum endpoint (Duane-Hunt limit) in an EDS spectrum as an in-situ readout of the true landing energy on charging specimens - e.g. Newbury's recommendations, Galvan Josa, Castellano & Bertolino 2013 Rad. Phys. Chem. 88:32 (quantification of uncoated non-conductors using the Duane-Hunt limit), and standard textbook treatment (Goldstein et al. 4th ed.). What magnitude of charging does it detect reliably, what are its limitations (statistics at the endpoint, pulse pile-up faking counts above the endpoint, time-varying potentials), and is 'acquire a spectrum, check the endpoint equals the set beam energy, plus stable count rate across replicates' an accepted accept/reject protocol for data from a possibly-charging specimen?

For every claim cite specific peer-reviewed papers, NIST publications, or authoritative textbook chapters with DOIs where they exist, give quantitative numbers wherever the literature provides them, and note honestly where the literature is silent or where values conflict.

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: paper_search
info.description:
Search for papers in Google Scholar for you to look at.

Can be called repeatedly with identical parameters to retrieve more results (max 2 repeats).
A short summary of the retrieved papers will be returned, but to examine the full content of each paper,
you must use the gather_evidence tool.

query.description:
A Google Scholar search query, which can be a specific phrase, complete sentence,
or general keywords, e.g. 'machine learning for immunology'. Also can be
given search operators like 'author:'.
query.title: Query

min_year.description:
filter for minimum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.
min_year.title: Min Year

max_year.description:
filter for maximum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.
max_year.title: Max Year

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: open_targets_search
info.description:
Search for disease-target associations from OpenTargets database.

Adds new disease-target association data to the state and returns top search results.

disease_names.description:
List of disease names to search for.
Usage:
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Returns top targets for Alzheimer's
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's", "Diabetes"], target_names = ["PSEN1"] ->
    Filters for only PSEN1-Alzheimer's/Diabetes evidence
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Filters for Alzheimer's disease-target pairs treated by Aducanumab

target_names.description:
List of target names to search for.
Usage:
target_names = ["BACE1"] ->
    Returns top diseases associated with BACE1
target_names = ["BACE1", "APP"], disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Filters for only these target-Alzheimer's pairs
target_names = ["BACE1"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Filters for BACE1 disease pairs treated by Aducanumab
target_names.title: Target Names

drug_names.description:
List of drug names to generate or filter results.
Usage:
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Returns all disease-target pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"], disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Filters for Alzheimer's pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"], target_names = ["BACE1"] ->
    Filters for BACE1 disease pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names.title: Drug Names

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):

        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1

        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing

        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.

Use the tools to answer the question: Context: Our lab performs standards-based quantitative SEM-EDS (k-ratio protocol, NIST DTSA-II) at E0 = 5 keV on a Thermo Fisher Apreo FE-SEM with an EDAX Octane Plus SDD (takeoff angle 35 degrees). One standard is an UNCOATED bulk single-crystal MgO wafer (10 x 10 x 0.5 mm, epi-polished, mounted on a grounded aluminum stub, silver/carbon paint border planned at the edges). Our carbon evaporation coater is unavailable for two months. Scope: SEM / EPMA / electron-irradiation physics of BULK insulators and thin insulating films only; exclude TEM entirely.

Questions:

(1) DEPTH OF ELECTRON PENETRATION AND TRAPPED CHARGE IN CHARGING INSULATORS. What does the peer-reviewed literature say about how deep primary-beam electrons penetrate and where the injected charge actually comes to rest in an electron-irradiated bulk insulator? Cover: (a) the initial implantation depth versus beam energy (electron range scaling); (b) the depth DISTRIBUTION of trapped charge - the dynamic double layer picture (thin positive surface layer from secondary-electron escape over a deeper negative space-charge layer near the end of range), e.g. Melchinger & Hofmann 1995 J. Appl. Phys. 78:6224 'Dynamic double layer model'; Cazaux's analyses of internal fields and charge distributions (e.g. J. Appl. Phys. 59:1418, 1986); self-consistent charge-transport simulations such as the flight-drift model (Touzin, Goeuriot, Guerret-Piecourt, Juve, Treheux, Fitting, J. Appl. Phys. 99:114110, 2006) and Fitting's related work; (c) the SELF-REGULATION of landing energy: as negative surface potential builds, the landing energy falls toward the second total-yield crossover E2 so the penetration depth shrinks toward the range at E2 - published statements and measurements of this steady state; (d) experimental methods that measured trapped-charge depth or surface potential (electron-mirror method, Kelvin probe, x-ray/spectral methods, Duane-Hunt endpoint shifts) with quantitative example numbers.

(2) GROUNDING FROM BELOW: CONDUCTIVE LAYER UNDER A THIN INSULATOR INSTEAD OF A TOP COAT. Is there published work on analyzing or imaging uncoated insulators by placing the conductor UNDERNEATH - i.e., thin insulating films or sections on grounded conductive substrates charging far less than bulk insulators? Cover the physics quantitatively: capacitive scaling of surface potential with dielectric thickness over a ground plane (V proportional to thickness for a given trapped areal charge); electron-beam-induced (radiation-induced) conductivity within the irradiated volume allowing deposited charge to leak to a substrate that lies within or near the interaction volume; the condition that the beam range reach or approach the conductive layer; evidence from electron-beam lithography (insulating resist films ~0.1-1 um on grounded silicon wafers) and from SEM/EPMA practice (e.g., thermal SiO2 films on Si imaged/analyzed uncoated; thin sections on conductive substrates). Also: any work on deliberately BURIED conductive layers (implanted or deposited interlayers) for charge mitigation in SEM samples, and the known failure modes (fluorescence of the buried layer by X-rays generated above it; changed backscattering when the substrate is inside the interaction volume; thin-film versus bulk matrix-correction differences).

(3) MgO SPECIFICALLY AT LOW BEAM ENERGY. MgO has one of the highest secondary-electron yields of any material (used for exactly that property in plasma display panels). What are the measured secondary-electron yield curves (delta_max, E_max) and total-yield crossover energies E1 and E2 for MgO (single crystal, thin film, and degraded/contaminated surfaces), e.g. Whetten & Laponsky's classic measurements and later compilations (Joy's database of electron-solid interactions; Cazaux's reviews)? At E0 = 5 keV, does bulk single-crystal MgO sit ABOVE unity total yield (net positive, self-limiting few-volt positive charging - benign for EDS) or below it (negative charging by kilovolts)? How strongly do surface contamination, hydroxylation, and electron-beam conditioning shift delta and E2 for MgO? Any direct measurements of MgO surface potential or charging behavior under keV electron beams (including in SEM), and any published SEM-EDS or EPMA analyses of uncoated MgO?

(4) THE DUANE-HUNT ENDPOINT AS A CHARGING GAUGE. Published validation of using the bremsstrahlung continuum endpoint (Duane-Hunt limit) in an EDS spectrum as an in-situ readout of the true landing energy on charging specimens - e.g. Newbury's recommendations, Galvan Josa, Castellano & Bertolino 2013 Rad. Phys. Chem. 88:32 (quantification of uncoated non-conductors using the Duane-Hunt limit), and standard textbook treatment (Goldstein et al. 4th ed.). What magnitude of charging does it detect reliably, what are its limitations (statistics at the endpoint, pulse pile-up faking counts above the endpoint, time-varying potentials), and is 'acquire a spectrum, check the endpoint equals the set beam energy, plus stable count rate across replicates' an accepted accept/reject protocol for data from a possibly-charging specimen?

For every claim cite specific peer-reviewed papers, NIST publications, or authoritative textbook chapters with DOIs where they exist, give quantitative numbers wherever the literature provides them, and note honestly where the literature is silent or where values conflict.

Abstract:
To study the impact of oxygen vacancies on spin-polarized transport, we have computed the electronic and transport properties of single (F centers) and paired (M centers) oxygen vacancies using density functional theory. These point defects can generate barrier heights as low as 0.4V for FeCo electrodes irrespective of the defect's spatial position within the barrier, and of the orientation of the M center. These defects promote a strong decrease in the conductance of the spin up channel in the magnetic tunnel junctions (MTJ)'s parallel (P) magnetic state that mainly accounts for an order-of-magnitude drop in TMR, from about 10000$\%$ in the ideal case toward values more in line with experiment. When placed in the middle layer of the MgO barrier, the F center introduces additional P $\uparrow$ transmission away from the $\Gamma$ point. This scattering lowers TMR to 145$\%$. In contrast, the M center merely broadens this transmission around $\Gamma$, thereby boosting TMR to 315$\%$. Rotating a M center so as to partly point along the transmission direction sharpens transmission around $\Gamma$, further increasing TMR to 1423$\%$. When these defects are placed at the MTJ interface, the transmission and ensuing TMR, which reaches $\approx$ 4000$\%$, suggest that such junctions behave as would an ideal MTJ, only with a much lower barrier height. Our results thus theoretically reconcile the concurrent observations of high TMR and low barrier heights, such as post-deposition oxidation of metallic Mg, which can generate oxygen vacancies at the lower MTJ interface, and annealing which can promote M centers over F centers.

Abstract:
ABSTRACT Charging effect frequently occurs when characterizing nonconductive materials using electrons as probes and/or signals and can impede the acquisition of useful information about the material under investigation. It is not adequate to investigate it merely by experiments, but theoretical investigations, for which the Monte Carlo method is a suitable tool, are also necessary. In this paper we review Monte Carlo simulations and selected experiments, intending to provide general insight into the charging effects induced by electron beam irradiation. We will introduce categories of the charging effect, the theoretical framework that is adopted in Monte Carlo modeling of the charging effect and present some typical simulation results. At last, with the knowledge on charging effect imparted by the above contents, we will discuss the measures that can be used for minimizing it. Graphical Abstract

Abstract:
Insulating materials are frequently used in spacecraft's structure and especially as thermal blanket which are protecting the electronic devices. Their behavior in relation to an electron beam irradiation due to space environment must be clearly elucidate. For example, when the electron beam is irradiated to the material, it charged up and a large electric potential difference generate between the charged and uncharged surfaces. If the difference in potential becomes very large, a discharge sometimes occurs between them. Such discharge is very harmful for the spacecraft. Therefore, at designing stage of spacecraft, it is important to understand the charging characteristics of the surface material of the spacecraft. In this paper, we focused on the charge accumulation in the materials under an irradiation of high energy electron beam. In the experiments, some fluorine materials are used which are ordinary used for the spacecraft. Judging from the measurement results, it was found that the amounts of accumulated electrons gradually decreased ever during an electron beam irradiation. In addition, we tried to explain for this phenomenon using an idea of RIC (Radiation Induced Conductivity).

## pqac-00000000

From text 'cazaux2006charginginscanning pages 3-5'.

Jacques Cazaux. Charging in scanning electron microscopy "from inside and outside". Scanning, 26 4:181-203, Dec 2006. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/sca.4950260406, doi:10.1002/sca.4950260406. This article has 145 citations.

Cazaux describes charging as a dynamic, depth-dependent double-layer process. Incident primary electrons generate electron–hole pairs throughout their penetration range R. Low-energy secondary electrons can escape only from a shallow region characterized by an escape depth or positive-layer thickness s (approximately related to the maximum escape depth r), leaving behind positive charge near the surface. Electrons that do not escape are transported deeper and may become trapped, producing an excess negative space-charge region extending toward the end of the primary-electron range R. Thus, when R is much larger than r—as for sufficiently high beam energies—the positive surface layer is thin while the negative layer is much thicker and deeper. Even if the integrated positive and negative charges are equal, their spatial separation creates a dipole and a nonzero, often positive, surface potential with an S-shaped depth profile. Charging is self-regulating: the resulting electrostatic field and surface potential modify secondary-electron escape and retard incoming primary electrons, reducing their landing energy and thereby lowering the secondary-electron yield. Irradiation consequently evolves toward a steady condition in which charge currents balance; the landing energy is driven toward the relevant crossover condition, ultimately associated with the second crossover E2 at higher-energy transitions.

Most relevant evidence (with ids):

## pqac-00000014

From text 'newbury2000measuresforspectral pages 1-2'.

Dale E. Newbury. Measures for spectral quality in low-voltage x-ray microanalysis. Scanning, 22 6:345-51, Nov 2000. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/sca.4950220602, doi:10.1002/sca.4950220602. This article has 18 citations.

The excerpt identifies the Duane–Hunt bremsstrahlung endpoint as a diagnostic for charging in low-voltage SEM/EDS. The endpoint is the maximum bremsstrahlung photon energy and should correspond to the effective electron landing energy; charging changes the specimen electric field and can decelerate subsequent incident electrons, thereby shifting the effective excitation/endpoint energy. In practice, the true endpoint should not be taken as the highest channel containing counts. Detector resolution broadening and pulse pile-up can produce counts above the physical endpoint, so the continuous bremsstrahlung slope is extrapolated to zero counts to estimate the limit. Endpoint determination is therefore statistically difficult, particularly because the high-energy tail contains few counts and because instrumental artifacts mimic above-endpoint signal. Most importantly, a satisfactory static Duane–Hunt limit does not rule out dynamic charging: time-dependent potentials can vary during spectral accumulation while leaving an apparently acceptable endpoint. The article recommends time-series measurements or dynamic energy windows that continuously monitor count rates. Thus, the excerpt supports using endpoint behavior as a charging diagnostic and possible landing-energy indicator, but not as a standalone accept/reject protocol for spectra from charging insulators. Quantitative and even qualitative results may remain unreliable when charging varies during acquisition; conductive coatings or a conducting-grid method are suggested when charging is problematic.

The excerpt treats the Duane-Hunt limit—the high-energy endpoint of the electron bremsstrahlung continuum—as a practical indicator of charging in low-voltage EDS. Charging changes the effective electron landing energy, so monitoring the observed bremsstrahlung endpoint provides evidence of the specimen potential and its variation during irradiation; in principle, the endpoint displacement can be used to infer the instantaneous landing energy relative to the nominal beam energy. The article emphasizes that endpoint and peak-ratio behavior should be followed over time rather than inferred from one long acquisition. A sequence of short spectra allows the analyst to inspect both the Duane-Hunt limit and relative peak heights for time-dependent charging distortions. ## pqac-00000021

From text 'rau2008mechanismsofcharging pages 7-8'.

URL: https://doi.org/10.1134/s1063783408040057, doi:10.1134/s1063783408040057. This article has 82 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt provides a charging model directly relevant to thin insulating films on grounded conductive substrates. Electron irradiation produces positive charge near the surface through secondary-electron emission and negative charge deeper in the insulator from implanted primary electrons, forming a double layer. The resulting internal electric field separates nonequilibrium carriers and drives a radiation-induced current, IRIC. Importantly for a film on silicon or another grounded substrate, charge can leave through surface and bulk leakage currents IL toward the grounded substrate; these currents reduce charge accumulation and therefore can reduce the surface potential compared with a bulk insulator. The total current balance is written as I0 = Iσ + IQ + IL, where Iσ is emitted-electron current, IQ is the charging or displacement current, and IL is leakage to ground. The approximate surface-potential expression explicitly includes the sample thickness h in the denominator, indicating capacitive scaling: for comparable charge distributions and material permittivity, decreasing film thickness lowers the potential generated by a given accumulated charge. The model uses ε0 and the relative permittivity εr; it gives εr(SiO2) = 3.9. The text also states that carriers drift and diffuse away from the irradiated region, further contributing to charge relaxation. These concepts apply qualitatively to SiO2-on-Si examined by SEM or EPMA and to electron-beam lithography resist films on grounded silicon wafers, although the excerpt does not report specific thin-film measurements.

The excerpt directly supports the electrostatic behavior of thin insulating films on conductive or grounded substrates. The electric field and potential are controlled not only by the trapped charge and specimen dimensions, but also by the geometry of nearby metallic surfaces held at fixed potential, including a grounded specimen holder. For an insulator covering a conductor, the external field from charge in the dielectric can be zero while a substantial internal field remains, especially near the metal–dielectric interface. Thus, a conductive substrate or coating can reduce externally observable charging and surface-potential signals without eliminating charge-related fields inside the film. The article explicitly notes that a thin insulator on a conducting material, such as SiO2 on Si, may have a surface potential too small to measure even when the local field is very high; a 100 Å film with a field of 10^5 V cm−1 would have only a 0.1 V voltage drop. The text explains this through the lack of mobile carriers in insulators, which prevents rapid neutralization. It also emphasizes that charging is time-dependent: the developing field changes incident-particle trajectories and emission processes, which subsequently alter the charge distribution. Nevertheless, the field can be large enough to drive migration of mobile species toward interfaces. Increasing insulating-layer thickness increases distortion of the relevant depth function and allows behavior to approach that of bulk insulating material. Abstract:
Metal oxides can act as insulators, semiconductors or metals depending on their chemical composition and crystal structure. Metal oxide semiconductors, which support equilibrium populations of electron and hole charge carriers, have widespread applications including batteries, solar cells, and display technologies. It is often difficult to predict in advance whether these materials will exhibit localized or delocalized charge carriers upon oxidation or reduction. We combine data from first-principles calculations of the electronic structure and dielectric response of 214 metal oxides to predict the energetic driving force for carrier localization and transport. We assess descriptors based on the carrier effective mass, static polaron binding energy, and Fröhlich electron-phonon coupling. Numerical analysis allows us to assign p and n type transport of a metal oxide to three classes: (i) band transport with high mobility; (ii) small polaron transport with low mobility; and (iii) intermediate behaviour. The results of this classification agree with observations regarding carrier dynamics and lifetimes and are used to predict 10 candidate p-type oxides.

Abstract:
Electronic transport in materials is governed by a series of tensorial properties such as conductivity, Seebeck coefficient, and effective mass. These quantities are paramount to the understanding of materials in many fields from thermoelectrics to electronics and photovoltaics. Transport properties can be calculated from a material’s band structure using the Boltzmann transport theory framework. We present here the largest computational database of electronic transport properties based on a large set of 48,000 materials originating from the Materials Project database. Our results were obtained through the interpolation approach developed in the BoltzTraP software, assuming a constant relaxation time. We present the workflow to generate the data, the data validation procedure, and the database structure. Our aim is to target the large community of scientists developing materials selection strategies and performing studies involving transport properties. Abstract:
Oxide electronic materials provide a plethora of possible applications and offer ample opportunity for scientists to probe into some of the exciting and intriguing phenomena exhibited by oxide systems and oxide interfaces. In addition to the already diverse spectrum of properties, the nanoscale form of oxides provides a new dimension of hitherto unknown phenomena due to the increased surface-to-volume ratio. Oxide electronic materials are becoming increasingly important in a wide range of applications including transparent electronics, optoelectronics, magnetoelectronics, photonics, spintronics, thermoelectrics, piezoelectrics, power harvesting, hydrogen storage and environmental waste management. Synthesis and fabrication of these materials, as well as processing into particular device structures to suit a specific application is still a challenge. Further, characterization of these materials to understand the tunability of their properties and the novel properties that evolve due to their nanostructured nature is another facet of the challenge. The research related to the oxide electronic field is at an impressionable stage, and this has motivated us to contribute with a roadmap on ‘oxide electronic materials and oxide interfaces’. This roadmap envisages the potential applications of oxide materials in cutting edge technologies and focuses on the necessary advances required to implement these materials, including both conventional and novel techniques for the synthesis, characterization, processing and fabrication of nanostructured oxides and oxide-based devices. The contents of this roadmap will highlight the functional and correlated properties of oxides in bulk, nano, thin film, multilayer and heterostructure forms, as well as the theoretical considerations behind both present and future applications in many technologically important areas as pointed out by Venkatesan. The contributions in this roadmap span several thematic groups which are represented by the following authors: novel field effect transistors and bipolar devices by Fortunato, Grundmann, Boschker, Rao, and Rogers; energy conversion and saving by Zaban, Weidenkaff, and Murakami; new opportunities of photonics by Fompeyrine, and Zuniga-Perez; multiferroic materials including novel phenomena by Ramesh, Spaldin, Mertig, Lorenz, Srinivasan, and Prellier; and concepts for topological oxide electronics by Kawasaki, Pentcheva, and Gegenwart. Finally, Miletto Granozio presents the European action ‘towards oxide-based electronics’ which develops an oxide electronics roadmap with emphasis on future nonvolatile memories and the required technologies. In summary, we do hope that this oxide roadmap appears as an interesting up-to-date snapshot on one of the most exciting and active areas of solid state physics, materials science, and chemistry, which even after many years of very successful development shows in short intervals novel insights and achievements. Guest editors: M S Ramachandra Rao and Michael Lorenz

Abstract:
Measuring the charge on a nearby space object during close proximity, servicing, and rendezvous and docking operations without requiring physical touch remains challenging despite decades worth of data on spacecraft charging and its risks. This paper proposes the means to identify the charge on a closely neighboring space object and its elemental composition by examining the X-ray spectrum generated by energetic electrons impacting the target. In particular, deconvolution of the bremsstrahlung X-ray continuum provides an estimate of the landing energy of the electrons. Knowing the initial electron energy, the potential difference between the source and the target is determined. Additionally, characteristic X-rays emitted during the process of energetic electron–matter impact allows the relative abundance of elements in the target to be determined. Spatial separations in the order of tens of meters are required between an electron gun and the corresponding detector to maximize the collection of the bremsstrahlung spectrum. This could be achieved with either the single-craft and deployable booms or through the use of two spacecraft. Electron beam energies of 40 kV are found to generate sufficient levels of X-rays for potential determination at over 10 m from the target and to determine the landing energy of the beam to within 0.14% using commercial X-ray detectors.

Abstract:
Abstract. Background: Charging of insulators is a complex phenomenon to simulate since the accuracy of the simulations is very sensitive to the interaction of electrons with matter and electric fields. Aim: In this study, we report model improvements for a previously developed Monte-Carlo simulator to more accurately simulate samples that charge. Approach: The improvements include both modeling of low energy electron scattering by first-principle approaches and charging of insulators by the redistribution of the charge carriers in the material with an electron beam-induced conductivity and a dielectric breakdown model. Results: The first-principle scattering models provide a more realistic charge distribution cloud in the material and a better match between noncharging simulations and experimental results. The improvements on the charging models, which mainly focus on the redistribution of the charge carriers, lead to a smoother distribution of the charges and better experimental agreement of charging simulations. Conclusions: Combined with a more accurate tracing of low energy electrons in the electric field, we managed to reproduce the dynamically changing charging contrast due to an induced positive surface potential.

## pqac-00000029

From text 'bagraev1980effectofcs pages 8-9'.

N.T. Bagraev and V.L. Borisov. Effect of cs and li atom adsorption on mgo: secondary emission and work function. Applications of Surface Science, 4:145-153, Mar 1980. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/0378-5963(80)90123-3, doi:10.1016/0378-5963(80)90123-3. This article has 1 citations.

This excerpt provides only limited quantitative secondary-electron-yield information for MgO and does not give a complete clean-surface parameter set (delta_max, E_max, E1, and E2). For the MgO + Cs system, it reports an estimated 50% increase in emitter efficiency near the energy of maximum secondary yield, while high secondary yields of approximately 30 are reported under the stated conditions. For MgO + Li, the first crossover energy is reported as 17–25 eV and is said to remain characteristic of MgO, indicating that Li changes electron escape conditions rather than bulk excitation conditions. The excerpt attributes increased yield at a reduced potential barrier to greater escape depths for low-energy electrons and a higher probability that slow electrons escape. It cites Whetten and Laponsky (1957), along with other references, but does not reproduce their MgO yield values. It also contains no numerical values attributed to Johnson and McKay, Choi, Scholtz, or other specific authors, and it does not mention Joy’s database. Therefore, the requested comparative literature values and Joy database parameters cannot be determined from these pages alone.

messages.content: Excellent! This is very important data. The Boughariou paper confirms that at 5 keV, MgO charges positively (σ₀ > 1). The intrinsic SE yield at 5 keV is about 2.5 at low current density, and the E_max is about 1.1 keV. At 30 keV, σ₀ = 0.6 (negative charging). Most relevant evidence (with ids):

## pqac-00000033

From text 'cazaux2006charginginscanning pages 2-3'.

Jacques Cazaux. Charging in scanning electron microscopy "from inside and outside". Scanning, 26 4:181-203, Dec 2006. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/sca.4950260406, doi:10.1002/sca.4950260406. This article has 145 citations.

Table I reports the second critical/crossover energy E°2 for several insulating materials. For NaCl and KCl, E°2 is much greater than 6 keV; for MgO it is much greater than 3.5 keV; for Al2O3 (alumina) it is approximately 20 keV; and for amorphous SiO2 (silica) it is greater than 3 keV. The table also shows that the maximum secondary-electron-emission yield δM depends strongly on the material and its preparation or crystalline state. MgO has a listed maximum yield of 23, with the table identifying the results as “W and L.” Thus, the maximum SE yield for the MgO specimen represented in the table is δmax (δM) = 23. The excerpt emphasizes that these values come from short-pulse experiments and that values obtained under permanent irradiation can differ significantly.

Abstract

  The purpose of this paper is to give some aspects of charging eﬀects on dielectric materials submitted to continuous electron beam
irradiation in a scanning electron microscope (SEM). When the dielectric is irradiated continuously, the so-called total yield approach
(TYA) used to predict the sign of the charge appeared on electron irradiated insulators fails because the charge accumulated in the dielec-
tric interferes with the electrons emission processes. Based on previous experimental and theoretical works found in the literature, an
analysis of the evolution of the electron yield curves r = f(E0) of insulators during irradiation is given. The aim of this work is ﬁrstly
to determine experimentally the second crossover energy E2C under continuous electron irradiation (charging conditions) and secondly
to demonstrate that the charge balance occurs at this beam energy and not at E2 the energy deduced from non-charging conditions (pulse
primary electron beam experiments) as commonly asserted. It is however possible to apply the TYA by substituting the critical energy E2
for E2C. The experimental procedure is based on simultaneous time dependent measurements of surface potential, leakage current and
displacement current. The study underlines the diﬀerence between the landing energy of primary electrons EL at the steady state and the
second crossover energy, E2C, for charged samples. Some preliminary results are also obtained concerning the inﬂuence of the incident
beam density on the energy E2C. The samples used for this study are PMMA, polycrystalline silicone dioxide (p-SiO2), polycrystalline
alumina (p-Al2O3) and soda lime glass (SLG).

info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.

if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,

search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the

info.description:

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: Context: Our lab performs standards-based quantitative SEM-EDS (k-ratio protocol, NIST DTSA-II) at E0 = 5 keV on a Thermo Fisher Apreo FE-SEM with an EDAX Octane Plus SDD (takeoff angle 35 degrees). One standard is an UNCOATED bulk single-crystal MgO wafer (10 x 10 x 0.5 mm, epi-polished, mounted on a grounded aluminum stub, silver/carbon paint border planned at the edges). Our carbon evaporation coater is unavailable for two months. Scope: SEM / EPMA / electron-irradiation physics of BULK insulators and thin insulating films only; exclude TEM entirely.

Questions:

(1) DEPTH OF ELECTRON PENETRATION AND TRAPPED CHARGE IN CHARGING INSULATORS. What does the peer-reviewed literature say about how deep primary-beam electrons penetrate and where the injected charge actually comes to rest in an electron-irradiated bulk insulator? Cover: (a) the initial implantation depth versus beam energy (electron range scaling); (b) the depth DISTRIBUTION of trapped charge - the dynamic double layer picture (thin positive surface layer from secondary-electron escape over a deeper negative space-charge layer near the end of range), e.g. Melchinger & Hofmann 1995 J. Appl. Phys. 78:6224 'Dynamic double layer model'; Cazaux's analyses of internal fields and charge distributions (e.g. J. Appl. Phys. 59:1418, 1986); self-consistent charge-transport simulations such as the flight-drift model (Touzin, Goeuriot, Guerret-Piecourt, Juve, Treheux, Fitting, J. Appl. Phys. 99:114110, 2006) and Fitting's related work; (c) the SELF-REGULATION of landing energy: as negative surface potential builds, the landing energy falls toward the second total-yield crossover E2 so the penetration depth shrinks toward the range at E2 - published statements and measurements of this steady state; (d) experimental methods that measured trapped-charge depth or surface potential (electron-mirror method, Kelvin probe, x-ray/spectral methods, Duane-Hunt endpoint shifts) with quantitative example numbers.

(2) GROUNDING FROM BELOW: CONDUCTIVE LAYER UNDER A THIN INSULATOR INSTEAD OF A TOP COAT. Is there published work on analyzing or imaging uncoated insulators by placing the conductor UNDERNEATH - i.e., thin insulating films or sections on grounded conductive substrates charging far less than bulk insulators? Cover the physics quantitatively: capacitive scaling of surface potential with dielectric thickness over a ground plane (V proportional to thickness for a given trapped areal charge); electron-beam-induced (radiation-induced) conductivity within the irradiated volume allowing deposited charge to leak to a substrate that lies within or near the interaction volume; the condition that the beam range reach or approach the conductive layer; evidence from electron-beam lithography (insulating resist films ~0.1-1 um on grounded silicon wafers) and from SEM/EPMA practice (e.g., thermal SiO2 films on Si imaged/analyzed uncoated; thin sections on conductive substrates). Also: any work on deliberately BURIED conductive layers (implanted or deposited interlayers) for charge mitigation in SEM samples, and the known failure modes (fluorescence of the buried layer by X-rays generated above it; changed backscattering when the substrate is inside the interaction volume; thin-film versus bulk matrix-correction differences).

(3) MgO SPECIFICALLY AT LOW BEAM ENERGY. MgO has one of the highest secondary-electron yields of any material (used for exactly that property in plasma display panels). What are the measured secondary-electron yield curves (delta_max, E_max) and total-yield crossover energies E1 and E2 for MgO (single crystal, thin film, and degraded/contaminated surfaces), e.g. Whetten & Laponsky's classic measurements and later compilations (Joy's database of electron-solid interactions; Cazaux's reviews)? At E0 = 5 keV, does bulk single-crystal MgO sit ABOVE unity total yield (net positive, self-limiting few-volt positive charging - benign for EDS) or below it (negative charging by kilovolts)? How strongly do surface contamination, hydroxylation, and electron-beam conditioning shift delta and E2 for MgO? Any direct measurements of MgO surface potential or charging behavior under keV electron beams (including in SEM), and any published SEM-EDS or EPMA analyses of uncoated MgO?

(4) THE DUANE-HUNT ENDPOINT AS A CHARGING GAUGE. Published validation of using the bremsstrahlung continuum endpoint (Duane-Hunt limit) in an EDS spectrum as an in-situ readout of the true landing energy on charging specimens - e.g. Newbury's recommendations, Galvan Josa, Castellano & Bertolino 2013 Rad. Phys. Chem. 88:32 (quantification of uncoated non-conductors using the Duane-Hunt limit), and standard textbook treatment (Goldstein et al. 4th ed.). What magnitude of charging does it detect reliably, what are its limitations (statistics at the endpoint, pulse pile-up faking counts above the endpoint, time-varying potentials), and is 'acquire a spectrum, check the endpoint equals the set beam energy, plus stable count rate across replicates' an accepted accept/reject protocol for data from a possibly-charging specimen?

For every claim cite specific peer-reviewed papers, NIST publications, or authoritative textbook chapters with DOIs where they exist, give quantitative numbers wherever the literature provides them, and note honestly where the literature is silent or where values conflict.

Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.

I'll create a comprehensive plan to address this multi-part question about electron-beam charging physics in SEM/EPMA, focusing on bulk insulators, grounding strategies, MgO specifically, and the Duane-Hunt endpoint as a charging diagnostic.

messages.content:
Plan registered and formatted correctly, with some modifications:
{
  "objectives": [
    {
      "id": 1,

To study the impact of oxygen vacancies on spin-polarized transport, we have computed the electronic and transport properties of single (F centers) and paired (M centers) oxygen vacancies using density functional theory. These point defects can generate barrier heights as low as 0.4V for FeCo electrodes irrespective of the defect's spatial position within the barrier, and of the orientation of the M center. These defects promote a strong decrease in the conductance of the spin up channel in the magnetic tunnel junctions (MTJ)'s parallel (P) magnetic state that mainly accounts for an order-of-magnitude drop in TMR, from about 10000$\%$ in the ideal case toward values more in line with experiment. When placed in the middle layer of the MgO barrier, the F center introduces additional P $\uparrow$ transmission away from the $\Gamma$ point. This scattering lowers TMR to 145$\%$. In contrast, the M center merely broadens this transmission around $\Gamma$, thereby boosting TMR to 315$\%$. Rotating a M center so as to partly point along the transmission direction sharpens transmission around $\Gamma$, further increasing TMR to 1423$\%$. When these defects are placed at the MTJ interface, the transmission and ensuing TMR, which reaches $\approx$ 4000$\%$, suggest that such junctions behave as would an ideal MTJ, only with a much lower barrier height. Our results thus theoretically reconcile the concurrent observations of high TMR and low barrier heights, such as post-deposition oxidation of metallic Mg, which can generate oxygen vacancies at the lower MTJ interface, and annealing which can promote M centers over F centers.
